title: Quantum Computing Is Getting Real. Developers Have An Opportunity.
excerpt: While quantum hardware keeps evolving, quantum software has gone much further than many realize
content:
Every computing transition follows the same pattern. Mainframes needed compilers. The internet needed browsers and application frameworks. Mobile needed SDKs. In each case, hardware created the possibility, and software created the access. Quantum computing is no different, yet the public conversation has been dominated by qubit counts and error-correction milestones, as if the machines will simply arrive pre-loaded with value.

While quantum hardware keeps evolving, quantum software has gone much further than many realize. Every enterprise use case now under serious evaluation, including portfolio optimization in finance, molecular simulation in pharma and chemistry, logistics and scheduling, materials design and cryptographic risk assessment, depends on software that translates a business or research problem into something a quantum processor can execute, and translates the result back into something a business can use. That translation layer is where the engineering work and the real quantum career opportunity sit. It is also where developers, not physicists, can do most of the building.

Classical Code and Quantum Code Are Not the Same Discipline

For developers new to the field, there are of course some differences between the disciplines. Classical programs manipulate deterministic bits whereas quantum programs manipulate probabilistic amplitudes across superposition and entanglement. Most answers only emerge after many repeated executions or ‘shots’, not one. There is no equivalent of a print statement mid-execution measuring a qubit collapses its state. Quantum debugging relies on simulators and statistical analyses rather than step-through inspection. Unlike classical code, which mostly runs unmodified across hardware, quantum programs must account for the physical constraints of the processor they target: qubit connectivity, gate fidelity, coherence time.

Classical concept Quantum equivalent
Bit (0 or 1) Qubit (superposition of |0> and |1>)
Deterministic output Probability distribution over outcomes
Debugging via logs and breakpoints Statistical sampling across repeated runs

None of this makes quantum programming inaccessible; it makes it a genuinely different discipline, closer in spirit to early classical computing, when developers also had to reason close to the hardware. What has changed is how much of that burden a developer must carry personally.

The Quantum Stack Is Further Along Than Most Developers Assume

Quantum software has quietly gone through the same maturation classical software went through decades ago: from hand-written machine instructions to compilers, high-level languages and reusable libraries. Today’s quantum development platforms, including high-level languages like Classiq’s Qmod, enable engineers to describe what a program should accomplish (the functional intent) rather than hand-assembling gate-level circuits qubit by qubit. A compiler handles the translation to a specific hardware backend automatically – the same separation of concerns that made classical software scalable. Each additional layer of abstraction, from gate-level circuits to functional models to natural-language agents, has lowered the entry barrier a little further and widened the pool of developers who can realistically contribute.

In practice, quantum computing software engineering workflows can look like this: a developer defines the problem and quantum logic in a high-level language such as Qmod; a compiler can turn that model into a circuit of quantum operations optimized for a specific target QPU; the resulting program runs on a simulator, on quantum hardware, or both, executed many times to build up a statistical result; and classical software handles everything around it – orchestration, data preparation and interpreting what the measurements mean for the business problem at hand. Writing quantum code, in other words, is one step in a pipeline that is mostly classical.

A minimal example makes this less abstract. Here is a Qmod function that creates a Bell pair, two qubits placed in superposition and then entangled:

@qfunc

def bell_pair():

    q0 = QBit()      # Create q0 in |0> state

    q1 = QBit()      # Create q1 in |0> state

    H(q0)            # Put q0 in superposition

    CX(q0, q1)       # Entangle q1 with q0

    return q0, q1    # Return entangled pair

H places the first qubit into superposition; CX entangles the second qubit with it. Measuring the pair always returns 00 or 11, never 01 or 10, the signature of entanglement. 

Agentic AI is now compressing the learning curve still further. Quantum AI agents can take a natural-language description of a problem and generate validated, hardware-portable quantum models directly, turning weeks of manual circuit construction into a task measured in minutes. In one recent collaboration between Classiq and Oracle, engineers used this approach to move from a simple prompt to a working 36-qubit application, tested through HPC-scale simulation on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, well before fault-tolerant quantum hardware is required. A demonstration of this workflow shows the increasingly practical, present-day reality of quantum development.

Why the Clock Is Now Running

In July 2026, IBM and the University of Chicago demonstrated quantum advantage using 70 logical qubits, completing in roughly 15 minutes a computation beyond the practical reach of leading classical simulation. Several hardware providers now have public roadmaps targeting commercial fault-tolerant systems before the end of this decade. The U.S. government is moving at a similar pace with the Department of Energy having committed $625 million to renew its five National Quantum Information Science Research Centers. The National Science Foundation recently announced more than $290 million for eight Quantum Leap Challenge Institutes, part of a broader federal push under the National Quantum Initiative to advance U.S. leadership in quantum science and technology.

Enterprises are responding in kind, with quantum moving out of R&D and into line-of-business teams. These teams need people who can build with the technology, not just explain it in a slide deck. The hiring signals are already visible with quantum software roles increasingly listed at companies that would not have had a quantum job description two years ago.

Where the Commercial Opportunity Currently Sits

The clearest near-term opportunities cluster around three problem types where classical computers hit real limits: optimization (routing, scheduling, portfolio and resource allocation), simulation (molecular and materials modeling for pharma, chemistry and energy), and machine learning augmentation. Add cryptographic risk assessment, and the addressable industries span finance, aerospace, automotive, logistics, energy, cybersecurity and life sciences. McKinsey’s 2026 Quantum Technology Monitor estimates quantum computing could create up to $2.7 trillion in economic value worldwide by 2035, a figure large enough to justify the current wave of enterprise investment, even before fault-tolerant hardware fully arrives.

A Global Race, Already Playing Out in Real Projects and Challenges

In the Global Quantum and AI Challenge, a year-long international program co-sponsored by Classiq, enterprises across sectors are already running quantum proof-of-concept projects tied to real operational problems, not academic exercises. Airbus is applying quantum methods to predictive aerodynamic modelling. Cleveland Clinic is simulating allosteric signal propagation inside biological molecules. E.ON is exploring quantum-enabled energy-grid distribution. HSBC is targeting credit-card fraud detection, and Volkswagen is working on vision-language-action models for autonomous driving and robotics. These are enterprise teams with production timelines, and they need software engineers who can engineer, build, test and iterate, not only researchers who can theorize.

Quantum Will Not Replace Classical Computing

Quantum computing is emerging as one part of a hybrid computational landscape, not a replacement for it. Classical processors will continue to handle control logic, data preparation and post-processing, working alongside QPUs, quantum-inspired algorithms running on classical hardware, and tight integration with high-performance computing infrastructure. The developers best positioned for this transition are likely not the ones abandoning classical expertise but the ones extending it.

Vehicle routing, a standard problem in Classiq’s own open-source library, illustrates this concept. A classical program first defines the problem: locations, distances and constraints such as each stop being visited exactly once, encoded as a cost function. A quantum algorithm, often QAOA, searches for low-cost solutions to that function using a quantum processor or simulator. Classical software then decodes the measurement results back into actual routes, checks that the constraints hold, and hands the result to the dispatch system. The quantum step is one stage in a pipeline that starts and ends in classical code, which is how most early enterprise quantum deployments are being built today.

The Opening Is Now

AI has already introduced real uncertainty into classical development careers, alongside real opportunity for those who adapt. Quantum computing is opening a comparable path at a moment when the barrier to entry, thanks to higher-level abstractions and AI-assisted development, is lower than it has ever been. For developers willing to invest now, quantum software engineering offers something increasingly rare in this AI-disrupted profession: a specialization still being defined, where enterprise demand is increasingly outpacing the supply of people who can deliver it. The on-ramp is not exotic: open-source quantum SDKs, free simulators and community programs like the Global Quantum and AI Challenge mean a first real project is closer than most classical developers assume. Developers who start now may also be the ones best equipped to make the case for quantum internally and influence their own employers to start preparing, before quantum readiness becomes quantum catch-up.
